newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Aghazadeh, last survivor of OPEC glory days.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Aghazadeh, last survivor of OPEC glory days.

text.p: Gholamreza Aghazadeh, whose successor as Iranian oil minister was announced on Tuesday, was the last survivor of the days when the OPEC cartel exercised real sway over world oil.
The 48-year-old ex-journalist will also be remembered as the man who guided reconstruction of Iran's war-torn oil industry and reopened it to foreign investors.

New Iranian President Mohammad Khatami on Tuesday nominated Bijan Namdar Zanganeh to replace Aghazadeh who now is expected to take a position in a mediating council headed by outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.

A tough but unfailingly courteous negotiator at Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries meetings, it was Agahazadeh's alliance with his Saudi counterparts Hisham Nazer and, latterly, Ali Naimi which ensured oil markets still took OPEC seriously.

But his dogged insistence that fellow members respect output quotas failed to stem the tide toward a free-for-all among producer nations already much further down the road in attracting foreign companies to boost production.
Aghazadeh's final OPEC meeting will probably go down as OPEC's last serious attempt to plug its failing quota system.
His 12 years in office were dominated by restoring Iran's crude output capacity lost after the 1979 revolution and the 1980-1988 war with Iraq which saw devastating attacks on Iranian oil facilities.

In 1985 Aghazadeh inherited an Iranian production rate of 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd), above the 1981 low tide-mark of 1.3 million but well adrift of the six million bpd achieved in the last years of the Shah.

Iran now produces 3.6 million bpd with surge capacity estimated at some four million. With Iraq sideline by Gulf War sanctions Iran is now the world's third biggest oil exporter behind Saudi Arabia and Norway.
Aghazadeh since 1990 had pushed to secure much needed foreign investment to ensure output capacity would be maintained as the country's ageing onshore oilfields matured and lost reservoir pressure.

He fought not just strong domestic opposition to allowing foreign firms to return to Iran but ran into increasingly severe U.S. trade sanctions which targeted Iran's oil industry as part of Washington's dual containment policy against Iran and Iraq.

At a conference in the Iranian city of Isfahan in 1991, state-owned National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) signed its first letter of intent with a foreign oil firm since the country's turbulent 1979 revolution.

But it took four more years -- regularly punctured with a series of additional U.S. sanctions -- for NIOC and the company, France's Total SA, to sign a $600 million groundbreaking deal to develop the Sirri E and A offshore oil and gas fields.
In 1995, NIOC released details of 10 oil and gas fields, gas distribution and refining projects that would be open to foreign firms under a "buy-back" formula.
Washington, accusing Iran of sponsoring terrorism, has done its best to prevent further steps by Tehran to attract foreign investment.

The U.S. blocked World Bank loans to Iran's oil sector, denied Tehran a role in an $8 billion consortium developing Caspian reserves, prevented U.S. Conoco from developing the Sirri fields and then stopped U.S. firms from lifting Iranian oil.

Sanctions culminated in U.S. President Bill Clinton signing the 1996 Iran Libya Sanctions Act which gave the president power to penalise even non-American firms that ventured to invest in Iran's oil sector.
But crude swaps deals with Kazakhstan and gas supply deals with Turkey, Turkmenistan and Pakistan were all testimonies to the growing international character of the Iranian petroleum ministry.
Aghazadeh's successor Zanganeh will be in place to award a $3.5 billion contract to further develop Iran's giant South Pars gas field to an international consortium headed by Total.
He will also have to face domestic political opposition to the gradual removal of state subsidies on oil products which is essential to dampen domestic use and ensure future crude export levels.
With the job comes the responsibility of ensuring the country's $18 billion annual petroleum export earnings which accounts for 40 percent of all government revenue and 80 percent of export revenue.
